claims.why: High-confidence regulatory, label or agency fact backed by an authoritative source.

claims.claim: Thymosin alpha-1 (thymalfasin) is a synthetically manufactured 28-amino-acid acetylated polypeptide identical to a naturally occurring human thymic peptide; it is described as activating toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9) signaling on dendritic cells, driving Th1 polarization and T-cell maturation as part of coordinated adaptive immune responses.
claims.why: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claims.claim: In the largest and most rigorous published human efficacy trial - TESTS, a multicentre, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trial in 1,106 adults with sepsis across 22 Chinese centers - subcutaneous thymosin alpha-1 every 12 hours for up to 7 days did not reduce 28-day all-cause mortality versus placebo (23.4% vs 24.1%; hazard ratio 0.99, 95% CI 0.77-1.27, p=0.93), and secondary/safety outcomes showed no significant differences between groups.
claims.why: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.

claims.claim: An earlier, smaller multicenter randomized controlled trial (ETASS, six Chinese hospitals, n=361 ICU patients with severe sepsis, 2008-2010) reported a numerically lower 28-day death rate with thymosin alpha-1 added to conventional therapy versus conventional therapy alone (26.0% vs 35.0%; relative risk 0.74, 95% CI 0.54-1.02), a difference that did not reach conventional statistical significance, alongside greater improvement in monocyte HLA-DR expression (an immune-function marker) in the treatment group.
claims.why: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.

claims.claim: Thymosin alpha-1 is marketed and discussed online as having been "long recognized for modifying, enhancing, and restoring immune function," with popular interest extending to autoimmune disease management, general inflammation reduction, cancer support, and longevity-adjacent uses such as long COVID; the only large, rigorous, placebo-controlled human trial identified for a systemic-immunomodulation indication (sepsis) found no mortality benefit, and consumer-facing sources themselves acknowledge that findings for these broader immune/longevity uses are based on small trials and that "more research is needed." No controlled human evidence for general immune optimization, anti-aging, or wellness use in healthy adults was identified in this review.
claims.why: Claim describes promotional or online certainty beyond the cited evidence.

claims.claim: LGD-3303 is a nonsteroidal, orally bioavailable SARM that binds the androgen receptor with high in vitro affinity (Ki = 0.9 nM) and potently activates AR-mediated transcription (EC50 = 3.6 nM, 134% efficacy relative to dihydrotestosterone), while showing much weaker affinity for the mineralocorticoid, glucocorticoid, and progesterone receptors (Ki = 1261, 581, and 136 nM respectively).

claims.claim: In castrated male rats (an androgen-deficiency model), oral LGD-3303 at 1 mg/kg/day completely prevented loss of levator ani muscle weight and acted as a partial agonist on prostate and preputial gland tissue; local tissue drug concentrations were reportedly higher in prostate than in the more strongly responding levator ani muscle, indicating the tissue selectivity is not explained by differential drug distribution. claims.claim: NIH's LiverTox reference describes a distinctive bland cholestatic drug-induced liver injury pattern documented with SARM use as a class: onset roughly 2-3 months after starting, presenting with fatigue, anorexia, dark urine, and jaundice, with moderate bilirubin elevation (reported 4-8 mg/dL initially) but only 2-5x-normal aminotransferase elevation, and a prolonged but usually self-limited course of about 1-6 months, occasionally with bilirubin cast nephropathy requiring temporary dialysis in severe cases. The compounds specifically named in LiverTox's case-report basis are ligandrol (LGD-4033), enobosarm/ostarine, vosilasarm/RAD-140, andarine, and YK-11; LGD-3303 is not individually named among the documented case reports in this reference, despite sharing the same androgen-receptor mechanism class.
claims.why: Support is user, community or case reports, not generalizable evidence.

claims.claim: The WADA Prohibited List's S1.2 anabolic-agents category prohibits "Selective androgen receptor modulators [SARMs, e.g. andarine, enobosarm (ostarine), LGD-4033 (ligandrol), RAD140, S-23 and YK-11]" using "including, but not limited to" language, so LGD-3303 falls within the prohibited SARM class as a chemical/pharmacological analog even though it is not individually named in this illustrative list. Independent anti-doping research has developed equine (horse) in vivo metabolite-profiling methods specifically to detect LGD-3303 administration, identifying a monohydroxylated metabolite with better detectability than the parent compound for doping-control testing.

claims.claim: LGD-3303 is sold online by research-chemical vendors carrying explicit "for research use only... not for human use" disclaimers, yet the same vendor product pages foreground preclinical rat muscle-sparing and receptor-potency data (e.g., "completely inhibits the loss of muscle weight," nanomolar Ki/EC50 figures) in ways that read as implied bodybuilding or performance benefit. No human efficacy or safety trial, case series, or FDA/DrugBank clinical data for LGD-3303 was located in this session. Muscle-building, bone-density, or other performance/wellness claims circulating in vendor and forum marketing for LGD-3303 are therefore not supported by human evidence and should not be treated as established benefits.
claims.why: Support is user, community or case reports, not generalizable evidence.

claims.claim: GSK2881078 is a synthetic, nonsteroidal selective androgen receptor modulator (SARM) — an indole-carbonitrile small molecule (CAS 1539314-06-1, PubChem CID 86709174) — that acts as an anabolic agent inducing anabolic effects in muscle via the androgen receptor, without approval as a drug product in any jurisdiction.

claims.claim: In a randomized, placebo-controlled, dose-escalation phase 1 study in healthy older men (1.0-4.0 mg/day) and postmenopausal women (0.35-1.5 mg/day) dosed for 28-56 days, GSK2881078 produced dose-dependent increases in total lean body mass at every dose level versus placebo; women gained roughly 3.39 kg and men roughly 1.76 kg of total lean mass by 8 weeks at studied doses. This is a healthy-volunteer pharmacodynamic finding, not evidence of clinical benefit (e.g., strength, function, or muscle-wasting outcomes) in a patient population.
claims.why: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claims.claim: In the same phase 1 study, all GSK2881078-dosed subjects showed reductions in HDL cholesterol (30-45% at the highest doses), and male subjects showed reversible reductions in total testosterone; changes reversed after stopping the drug. No serious adverse events were reported and the compound was described as generally well tolerated in this healthy-volunteer setting, but suppression of HDL cholesterol and androgen axis parameters are class-consistent safety signals for SARMs. An independent clinical-reference source (LiverTox) additionally reports that in this GSK2881078 trial, ALT rose above the upper limit of normal in over 50% of treated subjects (versus 13% of placebo) and above 5x ULN in 3% of treated subjects — a hepatic-transaminase-elevation signal not described in the primary paper's HDL/testosterone results and now added here as a distinct safety-critical signal.
claims.why: Human evidence exists but is not settled (was Moderate).

claims.claim: GSK2881078 was studied in a 13-week, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2a trial (NCT03359473) in 96 dosed COPD patients aged 50-75 with muscle weakness, using sex-specific doses (2 mg/day in men, 1 mg/day in women) alongside a home exercise program, with leg-press strength and DXA lean mass as primary/secondary endpoints. The trial completed in November 2019 with 77 of 96 participants completing and 10 discontinuations attributed to adverse events. The basis for the trial's existence, design and participant disposition in this packet is the trial registration records - the ClinicalTrials.gov entry and the sponsor's own study register, the latter now carrying no usable authority tier - which establish that the trial was conducted and how it was designed, but not what it found; no results from the primary publication have been retrieved and no efficacy outcome is asserted here. A secondary source (Wikipedia, not independently verified against the primary Thorax publication) states the drug increased muscle strength in men; this sex-specific efficacy framing and the full quantitative leg-press/DXA results remain unconfirmed and are not asserted here as established findings. A separate, independently accessed companion patient-reported-outcomes study of the same trial (Tabberer et al. 2024) reports that in a qualitative interview subsample (n=32), most participants described improvements in muscle strength and functional limitations and all reported a positive trial experience; this corroborates a general positive direction of participant-perceived effect but does not confirm, quantify, or sex-differentiate the efficacy result, and does not substitute for the primary trial's quantitative endpoints.
claims.why: Claim reports a negative or conflicting human finding.
